title: Why Growing MRR Doesn't Always Mean a More Profitable SaaS Business
linkedin:
A software business can post six months of steady MRR growth and still be quietly losing margin underneath it. Most owners don't see it until renewal season forces the conversation.

Here is the pattern we keep seeing in growing SaaS businesses in the one million to thirty million dollar revenue range. Monthly recurring revenue climbs. The board pack looks strong. But three cost lines move in the wrong direction at the same time, and none of them show up in the MRR number itself.

Support and customer success cost tends to scale with the number of accounts on the books, not the size of the revenue line. Ten new mid-market customers means ten new onboarding sequences and ten new sets of support tickets, whatever price tier they sit on.

Infrastructure cost moves with usage, not the invoice. When adoption deepens inside an existing account, the cost to serve that customer climbs faster than what they are paying, and nobody has repriced anything.

Annual prepayments can hide all of it. A year of cash sits in the bank from day one, while the true cost of servicing that customer builds gradually across the year. By the time renewal rolls around, the cash cushion has usually already been spent funding the next round of growth.

None of this means growth is the wrong goal. It means MRR was never built to answer the profitability question on its own.

A note for technology and software business owners on the east coast this month. If your monthly recurring revenue is growing steadily, it is worth checking that gross margin is actually keeping pace with it, because the two do not always move together.

The pattern we see often is straightforward. Support and customer success cost tends to grow with the number of accounts a business serves, not the size of the revenue line, so a broadening customer base can quietly push up the cost to serve each customer. Infrastructure cost moves with usage rather than what is invoiced, so as adoption deepens inside existing accounts, margin can compress without any pricing decision being made. And for businesses that take annual payment upfront, a healthy bank balance early in a contract can mask a servicing cost that is still building across the rest of the year.

None of this shows up clearly in a monthly recurring revenue figure on its own. It usually takes a proper look at gross margin by customer segment to see where it is actually heading.
